clue.text: Accommodation for officers isn't too special in mess

indicators.note: letters that are in a mess have been jumbled out of their proper order

parts.note: all fourteen letters, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone complaining that the officers' mess is a rather ordinary place to be housed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess' suggests an officers' mess, which fits the military surface, but here it simply signals rearranging the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Police stations house police officers, a punning reading of 'accommodation' for officers of the law rather than the army.

clue.text: Creating camps far apart, holding up rising increase in accessibility

indicators.note: one thing holding another has it inside its grip

parts.note: polarisation splits opinion into two opposing camps

indicators.note: in a down entry, something rising is read from the bottom upwards, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then turned around to PU

explanation.surface: A description of polarising politics somehow also making things more accessible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up rising' looks like one phrase about a rebellion, but 'up' is the fodder and 'rising' turns it over in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Popularisation makes a subject understandable and available to ordinary people, widening its reach.

clue.text: Pride is issue for her

parts.note: surface reading: some woman is troubled by her own pride, an issue she must deal with
setter's reading: a pride is a group of big cats, and 'issue' means offspring, so the pride is her family

explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' sounds like a problem, but in its older sense it means children; the female big cat raises cubs within a pride.
explanation.definitionFit: A pride is the social group of lions, and a female lion's cubs belong to it.

clue.text: Is spellbound? Oddly daft witch is fascinating

parts.note: read as 'is' bound by a spell: the two letters held inside a word for a magic spell

indicators.note: taking letters oddly means picking every other one, here the alternate set

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A puzzled onlooker wonders whether someone has been bewitched, given how captivating a silly witch is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is spellbound' reads as 'is enchanted', but literally means the word 'is' bound up in a spell. 'Oddly' here keeps the even-placed letters, a loose use of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A charismatic person exerts a compelling charm that draws others in, so they are captivating.

clue.text: In charge in Asian country, set up informal gathering

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting something up raises it so it reads from the bottom
one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: Laos, in South-East Asia
IC is the abbreviation for 'in charge'

explanation.surface: Someone in authority in an Asian country organises a casual get-together.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole construction, country with abbreviation inside, is reversed at the end, not just one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A social is a noun for a friendly party or casual get-together, often held by a club.

clue.text: Assigned a small place to sleep, overlapping with another

indicators.note: two words that overlap share a letter, so one copy of it is dropped where they meet

parts.note: taken as written
S is the standard abbreviation for small
a crib is a baby's bed
another place to sleep

explanation.surface: Someone is allotted a tiny sleeping space that encroaches on a neighbour's.
explanation.walkthrough: CRIB and BED share their B, so the two sleeping places overlap by one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascribe is to attribute or credit something to someone, so ascribed means attributed or assigned.

clue.text: Current occupant of seat is naughty child

parts.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current
a Member of Parliament holds a seat

explanation.surface: The present holder of a parliamentary seat is behaving like a badly behaved youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is a mischievous little devil, and by extension a cheeky, misbehaving youngster.

clue.text: Conspicuous reason for putting menu items on laptop?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: striking, worthy of attention

definitions.text: reason for putting menu items on laptop?
definitions.note: read as NO TABLE, a phrase rather than an adjective
definitions.meaning: second meaning, split as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests computer menus on a laptop, but the menu items are food and the lap is a literal lap, used when there is no table to eat at.
explanation.definitionFit: Something notable is remarkable enough to stand out, the same as conspicuous or prominent.

clue.text: Revolutionary leaders test bishop, say, as political adviser

indicators.note: a revolution overturns the existing order, so the letters are turned into a new arrangement

parts.note: eleven letters to rearrange
a bishop is an example of a chess piece, or man

explanation.surface: Radical party leaders put a churchman to the test as their adviser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bishop' looks ecclesiastical, but it is a chess piece; chessmen are called men.
explanation.definitionFit: An elder statesman is a retired senior politician whose experience makes them a respected counsellor.

clue.text: Parking car so, I disturbed pedestrian

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

indicators.note: things that are disturbed have been knocked out of place, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A driver admits that parking the car upset someone walking past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedestrian' reads as a noun for a walker, but the definition is the adjective meaning dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrian as an adjective means dull and uninspired, a synonym of prosaic.

clue.text: Excellent, like every part of RAF, but not army or navy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: first-rate, a dated exclamation of approval

definitions.text: like every part of RAF, but not army or navy
definitions.meaning: second meaning: each letter of RAF is an upper-case letter, while the two other services are printed in lower case

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests praising the Royal Air Force over the other services, but it is about typography: R, A and F are all upper-case letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital means first-rate in old British slang, and also an upper-case letter.

clue.text: Don't stand for this form of dishonesty

definitions.meaning: first meaning: recline rather than stay upright

explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't stand for this' reads as refusing to tolerate dishonesty, but splits into an instruction to recline and a word for a falsehood.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie is to be horizontal rather than upright, and a lie is also a deliberate falsehood.

clue.text: Never to be removed from home — a right to keep property accomplished

parts.note: being in means being at home
taken as written
a lien is a legal right to hold another's property until a debt is paid
able means skilled or competent

explanation.surface: Legal language about a skilled person's right to keep property at home that can never be taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: Inalienable rights cannot be taken away or transferred, so they can never be removed from their holder.

clue.text: Former PM introducing current measure with style in this town

indicators.note: one thing introducing others comes at the front, setting the order of the parts

parts.note: Lord North was British Prime Minister from 1770 to 1782
an amp is the unit of electric current
ton is fashionable style, as in 'bon ton'

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister brings electrical measurement and style to a town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Introducing' means the PM comes first and is followed by the other pieces. Northampton is a large town in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Northampton is the county town of Northamptonshire, so it fits a clue that asks for a town.

clue.text: Make a fresh start after employer rejected first person

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: one who employs a thing uses it
me is the first-person pronoun

explanation.surface: After being turned down by a boss, a jobseeker has to start over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Employer' looks like a boss, but here it is one who employs, or uses, something.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to begin again after a pause, picking up where one left off.

clue.text: Unparalleled order to stop being so inquisitive

definitions.text: order to stop being so inquisitive
definitions.note: read as PEER LESS, an instruction
definitions.meaning: second meaning, split as two words: a command to look curiously less often

explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer is an instruction to someone nosy to stop peering so much.
explanation.definitionFit: Something peerless has no peer or equal, which is what unparalleled means.

clue.text: Early-morning call always upset sick European

indicators.note: in a down entry, a word upset is tipped over so it reads from the bottom

parts.note: ever means always
ill means unwell
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: An early wake-up call always upsets an unwell European.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal, but here it turns EVER over to REVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Reveille is the bugle call that wakes soldiers at the start of the day.

clue.text: Make interesting observations as visitors

parts.note: surface reading: say clever, insightful things
setter's reading: look at interesting places, as tourists do

explanation.walkthrough: 'Observations' suggests remarks, but here it means literally looking at things, the way tourists view landmarks.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourists go round viewing famous attractions, which is exactly what this verb describes.

clue.text: Potentially earning as possible babysitter

indicators.note: potentially means 'could become', so these letters could be turned into something else

parts.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone sees childminding as a possible way to bring in some money.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandmother is a classic example of a family member who might look after the children.

clue.text: Number of Latin Americans giving short talks

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so each word drops its last letter

parts.note: two chats, one per talk

explanation.surface: A group of Latin Americans delivering brief lectures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is a dance number, not a count; the plural 'talks' supplies two chats, each losing its T.
explanation.definitionFit: The cha-cha is a ballroom dance from Cuba, a number danced to Latin American music.

clue.text: Stripped in exotic act in nightclub

definitions.note: cabaret is the entertainment in a nightclub, or the club itself

indicators.note: exotic means foreign and strange, so the letters are made unfamiliar by rearranging them
one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: the three letters rearranged
stripped means naked

explanation.surface: A striptease forms part of an exotic dancing act in a nightclub.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabaret is the floor show of songs and dances staged in a nightclub, and also such a club.

clue.text: Ornamental piece I put in last

indicators.note: a letter put in a word is inserted inside it

parts.note: final means last
taken as written

explanation.surface: A craftsman adds the decorative finishing touch at the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: A finial is a decorative knob or spike at the top of a spire, gable or bedpost.

clue.text: Awfully smart hi-tech system of the 80s

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters come out in a garbled order

parts.note: eleven letters, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: A scornful verdict on some flashy 1980s computer system.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Thatcher was UK Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990; her free-market politics bear her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Thatcherism was the political and economic doctrine that dominated British government in the 1980s.

clue.text: Reason for competitor's effortless progress for so long

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a free pass to the next round with no opponent

explanation.walkthrough: 'For so long' reads as a duration, but 'so long' is a casual farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: A bye lets a player advance without playing, and 'bye' is also short for goodbye.

clue.text: Have a line about game's unfortunate score

parts.note: to own is to have
a go is a turn or game
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A pundit comments on a match decided by an embarrassing goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is used loosely here: the a-and-line pair attaches to the game word rather than wrapping it.
explanation.definitionFit: An own goal is one a player accidentally scores against their own side, a misfortune in football.

clue.text: It's not on circular letter fellow duplicated

parts.note: the round letter
F is the abbreviation for fellow, here written twice

explanation.surface: Sending a chain letter to a colleague twice is unacceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circular letter' looks like a mailshot but is just the round letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Off is the opposite of on, said of a switched-off device or a cancelled event.

clue.text: For a period when classes are happening without one

indicators.note: without, in its old sense of outside, means wrapping around something

parts.note: in term, during the school or university teaching period
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A school timetable note about a period when lessons go on without someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it means outside, so IN TERM goes round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Interim describes a temporary arrangement lasting only for a limited time until something permanent follows.

clue.text: Meat dish, in general, following grouse

indicators.note: one word following another is written after it, which sets the order of the two parts

parts.note: a beef is a complaint, as is a grouse
the Duke of Wellington, the general who beat Napoleon at Waterloo

explanation.surface: A game-bird dish, with the meat broadly coming after the grouse course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like the game bird but is a complaint; 'in general' reads as 'broadly' but names the general.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef Wellington is fillet steak wrapped in pastry, a classic roast served as a main course.
